title: Kushmanda's Smile, Lakshmi's Nights
hookLine: night four: the list in the Devi Kavacha reaches Kushmanda, and in another way of keeping the festival, Durga's nights give way to Lakshmi's
carry: one goddess: durga clears, then lakshmi fills

lines: THE DEVI KAVACHA COUNTS HER OUT.
cards: There's a short hymn called the Devi Kavacha, the goddess's armor, which some people recite before the Devi Mahatmya. Partway through, it counts the goddess out like stairs. First, Shailaputri.
Second, Brahmacharini. Third, Chandraghanta. Fourth, Kushmanda.
And on, name after name, until it says these are the nine Durgas. In some homes that list becomes the festival's calendar: one form for each night.
But a second way of keeping Navaratri gives the first three nights to Durga, the middle three to Lakshmi, and the last three to Saraswati. By that count, night four is a hinge.

teach.b: Start with Kushmanda; you met her briefly on day ninety-four. The Kavacha only names her; it doesn't tell her story. But there's a story people tell.
Before anything existed there was only darkness, and the goddess smiled, and the world came out of that smile. It's a bright picture for the fourth night: creation beginning as a face lighting up.
Now the second way of counting. Durga's three nights cleared the road. Then, on night four, Lakshmi arrives: the goddess of good fortune, of plenty, of a household that has enough to share.
Earlier this year, the Sri Sukta asked her to come and stay.
Underneath both ways of counting is one Hindu teaching: the Devi is one, and she takes many forms.
Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati aren't three rivals taking turns. Many devotees see them as faces of the one Shakti: power, plenty, and wisdom.
Tradition even assigns the three parts of the Devi Mahatmya to Mahakali, Mahalakshmi and Mahasaraswati.
So the order of the nights is the order of a life: clear what blocks the way, then let good things in, then learn.
Some families have a homely version for tonight: before welcoming Lakshmi, they sweep the corners and light a lamp in a clean doorway, because Lakshmi, they say, comes to a home that's ready.
And what she brings isn't more stuff. It's enough: health, a full table, friends at it, a little to give away. Kushmanda's smile sits over all of it: in this story the good world begins with delight.

how: Some Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga named in the Devi Kavacha on each night of Navaratri; others, especially in parts of South India, give three nights each to Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati.

games.q: what does “navaratri as a nine-night curriculum” mean?
o: nine nights of fasting with the house kept closed

games.q: you keep Navaratri three nights at a time. Durga's three nights are done and the house is swept. who do you welcome on night four?
o: Durga again, for three more nights.
Lakshmi, goddess of good fortune and plenty.
games.why: in that scheme, the middle three nights belong to Lakshmi. clearing first, then filling. Saraswati's nights come last.

practice: Notice the room you're sitting in, the space around you and above you, the quiet between sounds, and let it feel roomy.
Then let one good thing into that room, a person you're grateful for, a meal you're glad of, something already given, and let it sit there and be enough.
If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, quietly with the breath.
